item.title: Rogers opens door to Democratic voters after El-Sayed’s primary victory: ‘There is still hope’
item.description: Mike Rogers appeals to Michigan Democrats after Abdul El-Sayed's primary win, saying those who feel unrepresented have a home with his campaign.
item.content:encoded:
Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers opened the door to Michigan Democrats on Friday after far-left progressive Abdul El-Sayed's primary victory, assuring them "there is still hope," adding they have a "home" with his campaign.

"If you're among the majority of Democratic voters that woke up on Wednesday feeling, well, hopeless, because the person who won does not represent your values, well, just know, there is still hope," Rogers said in a video posted on X Friday.

"Michigan deserves a senator who is ready to sit with you, hear from you and represent you."

El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in one of the nation's most closely watched Democratic primaries, setting up a November showdown with Rogers, who ran uncontested.

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Rogers addressed Democratic voters directly, casting his campaign as a home for those who feel their values are not reflected in El-Sayed's candidacy as he tries to court the hundreds of thousands of Democrats who voted for Stevens but may not feel comfortable voting for El-Sayed.

"The parents across Michigan who want an education system that sets up their kids for success, you have a home with us," he said. "To grandparents across Michigan who are heartbroken from watching their kids and grandkids leave the state, you have a home with us.

"To young people who are looking for real solutions to solve our housing affordability crisis, you have a home with us. To working families who don't want higher taxes and lower paychecks, well, you have a home with us."

Rogers also accused El-Sayed's campaign of promoting "anger, divisiveness, calls for violence" and views he said are out of step with Michigan voters.

"And to the vast majority of people across Michigan who do not want to throw their support behind a campaign filled with anger, divisiveness, calls for violence and the views that are out of touch with your values, well, you have a home with us," he said.

EL-SAYED'S THREAT AGAINST GOP RIVAL BACKFIRES AS CONSERVATIVES BRING RECEIPTS: 'IS DUBAI IN FLORIDA?'

"Over the next 90 days, I'm going to work hard to earn your trust, to earn your support and earn your vote," Rogers said. "We have a state to save, Michigan. Let's get to work."

Rogers' outreach to Democrats was praised by some conservatives and pundits on social media.

In a post on X, former DSA member Jake Altman wrote, "I voted for Biden. I voted for Harris. I will vote for Mike Rogers. I just donated to the campaign. This is not a time to sit on your hands. Stand up for the man who fights terrorists, not the one who sympathizes with them."

In another post on X, Democrats for Mike Rogers wrote, "Mike Rogers is meeting the moment. We’re putting country over party and voting for Mike Rogers in November. It’s never been more important. We must unite and defeat the extremism of Abdul El-Sayed and his allies."

El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former Wayne County health director who unsuccessfully ran for governor in 2018, has campaigned on Medicare-for-all and abolishing Immigration and customs enforcement. He has also been a vocal critic of Israel during its war with Hamas and has called Israel's actions in Gaza "genocide."

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: THE REPUBLICAN-LED VOTE THAT REVEALED DEMOCRATS' NEW DIVIDE ON ISRAEL

He would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected.

As some Democrats grapple with the direction of their party following El-Sayed's nomination, Rogers said the "fight is far greater than just left versus right."

"The fight is for the very soul of our nation," he said.

Fox News Digital reached out to El Sayed's campaign for comment.

item.title: Lindsey Graham's final mission to punish Putin clears Senate after yearlong fight
item.description: A sanctions bill targets Russia's oil and gas revenue with up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports and penalties on countries buying Russian energy.
item.content:encoded:
It’s taken well over a year of stops, starts, promises and derailments, but the Senate has at last advanced a bone-crushing package of sanctions against Russia, capping off one of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s biggest fights.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act sailed through the Senate on another colossal bipartisan vote and is now headed to the House. It has the backing of President Donald Trump, too.

It comes after personal lobbying from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week, who, hours after Graham’s memorial service in Washington, D.C., pleaded with lawmakers to put a check on Russian President Vladimir Putin.

GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION ADVANCES AS SENATE MOVES TO CRUSH PUTIN'S WAR MACHINE WITH RUSSIA, IRAN SANCTIONS

"Today, President Zelenskyy is watching from Ukraine, and Putin is watching from Moscow," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said on the Senate floor. "I would like to think that Lindsey Graham is watching, too."

The bill focuses on kneecapping Putin’s war machine by targeting Moscow’s top financial driver: oil and gas sales.

It also extends sanction authority against Iran that hampers funding to the country’s weapons and energy sectors as the administration and negotiators abroad seek to find a long-lasting peace agreement for the war in the Middle East.

There are also targeted sanctions against Putin, Russian officials and Russian military leaders, up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports and tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian energy, like China and India. And it gives Trump flexibility for when to turn off some aspects of the sanctions.

'A BIG EFFING DEAL': GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION MOVES FORWARD AFTER HIS DEATH

The tariff authority, however, threatened one last derailment of the package.

Sens. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Ron Wyden, D-Ore., initially held up the package over the issue and offered an amendment to solve the problem.

Paul, who has staunchly opposed Trump’s tariff strategy since he retook office, argued that slapping tariffs on superpowers working with Russia, like China, would only cause them to cozy up.

"These tariffs threaten to undermine America's strategic position in the world," Paul said. "Some naively think that the tariffs will get China to distance themselves from Russia, but it might be the opposite.

TRUMP ALLIES PUSH TO ARM PRESIDENT WITH NEW TARIFF WEAPON TO PUNISH COUNTRIES 'RIPPING OFF' AMERICA

"Recent history suggests that they will instead push Russia and China together," he continued. "China is not going to get this 100% tariff and say, ‘Oh, we're sorry, we're no longer going to cooperate with Russia.’"

Then came Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., who proved to be the last hurdle.

But after meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer Thursday, Warnock backed down after receiving a commitment that Trump’s tariff authority was indeed limited to just the top five countries purchasing oil and gas exports from Russia.

"We should not have to choose between putting a check on Putin's aggression and putting a check on this president's tariff regime," Warnock said. "That is a false choice, and it is one that I am not willing to accept."

item.title: North Korea expert warns US can 'never take their eye off' Kim Jong Un following missile test during Iran war
item.description: A North Korea expert said the U.S. can never take its eye off Kim Jong Un and the Korean Peninsula after North Korea test-fired a missile this week.
item.content:encoded:
A North Korea expert told Fox News Digital the United States "can never take their eye off" Kim Jong Un and the Korean Peninsula after Pyongyang test-fired a missile this week amid the ongoing conflict with Iran.

The launch of the short-range ballistic missile, which Japan said landed in the waters off North Korea’s east coast, unfolded Thursday ahead of joint military exercises to be conducted by the U.S. and South Korea later this month.

"There's this unsettled conflict on the Korean Peninsula. And Kim Jong Un, a very unpredictable leader that seeks attention, that is something the United States can never take their eye off," retired Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, a senior fellow at Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital Friday.

US SAYS NORTH KOREA MISSILE LAUNCH POSES NO IMMEDIATE THREAT, 'CONSULTING CLOSELY' WITH ALLIES

"So, we have all these challenges in the Middle East, these challenges with Russia and Ukraine, these challenges with China pressuring and trying to coerce Taiwan. You can never forget that the North Korean challenge to South Korea is sitting right there, and there are no constraints on Kim Jong Un," Montgomery added. 

"There's no version of an empowered elite or a population or a military that could unseat him. So, we should always keep our eye on him, pay attention to him and make sure we're constantly deterring any provocative behavior."

"We are aware of the missile launch and are consulting closely with our allies and partners," U.S. Indo-Pacific Command said after North Korea’s launch Thursday.

"Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory or to our allies," it added. "The United States remains committed to the defense of the U.S. homeland and our allies in the region."

Montgomery said Friday that "whenever North Korea does a ballistic missile launch, you have to think there's any of three countries that could be the intended recipient of the message. It could be the United States. It could be South Korea. It can be Japan, or it could be a mix."

MORE THAN HALF OF SOME US WEAPONS STOCKPILES USED IN IRAN WAR, RAISING CONCERNS ABOUT CHINA THREAT

He described how Japan recently test-fired a Tomahawk cruise missile in late July with the help of the U.S. Navy.

"Maybe this could be a signal back to them," Montgomery said. "South Korea and the United States are about to start the Ulchi Freedom series of exercises ... the most robust series of exercise we have there every August when conducted.

"Recently, there have been a lot of reports the United States has expended a large percentage of its theater ballistic missile defense weapons ... Patriot 3 and THAAD, in the conflict in Iran.

"Those are the kind of defensive systems that might be used against this weapon. Also, there's U.S. Navy standard missiles, which also have been depleted in the Middle East. In all those cases, North Korea could be signaling to any of the three countries or a mix of the three countries that we're still relevant, we matter and you need to pay attention to us."

Fox News’ Liz Friden contributed to this report.

item.title: Smart toilet seat could detect AFib in 30 seconds
item.description: The HARO EKG-seat by Hamberger Medical records a six-lead EKG in 30 seconds while you sit, scanning for atrial fibrillation and irregular heartbeat.
item.content:encoded:
Your next bathroom break could come with an unexpected bonus: a check of your heart rhythm. German medical technology company Hamberger Medical has developed the HARO EKG-seat. It looks like a regular toilet seat, but built-in sensors record an electrocardiogram, also called an EKG or ECG, while you sit.

After about 30 seconds, a connected smartphone app analyzes the reading for signs of an irregular heart rhythm, including possible atrial fibrillation. AFib is the most common type of irregular heartbeat, and millions of people may have it without realizing anything feels wrong. It sounds like the kind of idea someone dreamed up during a very long bathroom break.

However, the possibility of catching a silent heart condition during something you already do every day deserves attention. Here's what the early research reveals about how well the seat works and where its limits begin.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

A conventional medical EKG usually requires you to lie down while a medical professional places electrodes on your chest and other parts of your body. The HARO EKG-seat takes a different approach. Its sensors collect electrical signals from your body while you sit normally. The seat records a six-lead resting EKG and sends the information to its companion app through Bluetooth.

You do not need to attach sticky pads or remember to put on a wearable. You sit for about 30 seconds and let the seat do the work. Hamberger Medical says participants in its usability testing could operate the system without special instructions. The oldest participants in one reported study were in their 90s, according to published reports about the device. That simplicity may become one of its biggest strengths. Many health devices end up forgotten in a drawer after the novelty fades. A toilet seat is harder to forget.

The company tested the seat through what it calls the Hamberger Heart Study. Researchers compared the seat's six-lead EKG with a standard 12-lead medical EKG. Hamberger Medical reported a high level of agreement between the two systems when checking for AFib and other rhythm abnormalities.

That sounds encouraging, but there is an important limitation. The complete results have not been published in an independently peer-reviewed medical journal. Public reports also do not provide enough detail about the study's size, false alerts or performance across different groups.

Without those numbers, we cannot tell how often the seat might miss AFib or mistakenly warn someone whose heart rhythm is normal. For now, the results should be viewed as promising company-reported findings. They do not prove that the seat can replace a hospital EKG or a doctor's diagnosis.

AFib causes the heart's upper chambers to beat irregularly. Blood may then pool inside the heart, which can allow clots to form. A clot can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. The American Heart Association says AFib is linked to about five times the risk of stroke. Some people feel a racing heartbeat or fluttering in their chest. Others notice fatigue, dizziness or shortness of breath.

However, AFib can also arrive without obvious warning signs. A person may feel fine while the irregular rhythm comes and goes. That creates a detection problem. A brief EKG at a doctor's office may look normal if the AFib episode ended before the appointment. Doctors sometimes use longer-term monitors when they suspect an intermittent rhythm problem. A toilet seat that records readings regularly could provide more chances to capture an episode.

WEARABLE PATCH VIBRATES WHEN DANGER IS NEARBY

The American Heart Association estimates that about 5 million Americans currently live with AFib. It projects that more than 12 million could have the condition by 2030. Early detection can help doctors decide whether someone needs medication, additional monitoring or treatment to restore a normal rhythm.

Dr. Paari Dominic, a cardiac electrophysiologist, told the American Medical Association that earlier intervention can significantly improve outcomes. He noted that research supports pursuing normal rhythm within a year of detecting AFib in appropriate patients. However, a notification from a toilet seat should begin a medical conversation. It should never end one.

Age raises the likelihood of developing AFib. High blood pressure also plays a major role. Diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and certain heart conditions can increase the risk. Smoking and excessive alcohol use may contribute as well.

Heavy drinking can sometimes trigger an irregular heartbeat even in people without a known heart condition. Doctors often call this "holiday heart syndrome" because cases can rise during celebrations involving heavier alcohol use. People who already face a higher risk could benefit most from convenient monitoring. That decision should involve a cardiologist or another qualified medical professional.

A heart-monitoring toilet seat collects highly sensitive information, so its privacy protections deserve a close look. According to Hamberger Medical's app privacy policy, EKG processing happens locally on the connected phone or tablet. The company says readings are not sent to its servers. The app also lets you export a PDF report. Hamberger Medical recommends protecting the file with a password before sending it to someone else. However, your phone's backup settings may still upload app information to iCloud or Google Backup. The company notes that this depends on how you configured your device.

Before using any connected health product, check its backup settings and sharing options. You should also protect your phone with a strong passcode. For additional steps, see our guide on how to stop health and fitness apps from using your private data.

HEART CONDITION TIED TO LINDSEY GRAHAM'S DEATH CAN STRIKE WITHOUT WARNING — WHAT TO KNOW

The HARO EKG-seat does not currently appear to be available for purchase. Hamberger Medical previously said the device was sold exclusively through its official German online shop at approximately $2,870. CyberGuy reached out to Hamberger Medical to confirm current availability, pricing and whether the company plans to sell the EKG-seat in the United States, but did not hear back before our deadline.

The HARO EKG-seat shows how health monitoring could blend into your normal routine. That part is genuinely promising. The clinical report suggests the seat can record EKGs that cardiologists interpret with strong accuracy. However, the current app results do not support relying on its automated AFib classification alone.

A normal app reading should not convince you to ignore symptoms. An abnormal warning should lead to a conversation with a medical professional. Contact your doctor if you notice a racing or irregular heartbeat, recurring dizziness or unexplained shortness of breath. Chest pain or pressure may signal a medical emergency, so call 911 right away. Never start or stop heart medication because of a consumer device result. Your doctor may order a clinical EKG or longer-term monitoring before making a diagnosis.

There is something undeniably clever about turning an ordinary toilet seat into a heart monitor. It fits health screening into a routine that people already follow without reminders. The company-reported results sound encouraging, especially for a condition that may hide between doctor visits. Smart health technology works best when it helps you notice a concern sooner and gives your doctor useful information. It becomes dangerous when a gadget creates false confidence or replaces professional care.

Would you trust a smart toilet seat with your heart data if it could uncover a silent problem before your next doctor visit? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: NBA star Kyrie Irving got his apology, but four COVID-era athletes still waiting for theirs from the media
item.description: Beyond Kyrie Irving's apology from Stephen A. Smith, Novak Djokovic and three other athletes still await media accountability for their stance.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Mavericks star Kyrie Irving recently received an apology from ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith regarding his decision to remain unvaxxed during the pandemic, which cost him millions of dollars. For some, these statements were a welcomed piece of accountability not normally seen in the media. It also got me thinking about what other COVID-era athletes deserve apologies from the media, and recognition for their courage during a time in which being unvaxxed was essentially a crime in the eyes of the media.

STEPHEN A. SMITH ONLY SPEAKS UP ABOUT IMPORTANT SOCIETAL ISSUES ONLY WHEN IT'S POLITICALLY ACCEPTABLE

No athlete became more synonymous with the vaccine debate than the greatest tennis player of all-time, Novak Djokovic. (I like to refer to him as Novax when discussing this insane era of sports history).

Although Djokovic repeatedly rejected the label of being "anti-vaccine," he consistently maintained that medical decisions should remain a matter of personal choice. He consistently preached a message of bodily autonomy in regards to COVID-19.

In 2020, he stated, "I am opposed to vaccination if someone is forcing me to take a vaccine in order to travel." Two years later, following his deportation from Melbourne, Australia, home of the Australian Open, he reiterated, "I was never against vaccination, but I've always supported the freedom to choose what you put in your body."

Despite those statements, much of the media portrayed Djokovic primarily through the lens of vaccine opposition and as Djokovic said to "60 Minutes," "I was basically declared as a villain of the world."

"Time" magazine published articles including "Why Australians Are Furious About Anti-Vaxxer Novak Djokovic" and even wrote in an article, "The entire saga could easily have been avoided if Djokovic had been fully vaccinated." "Vanity Fair" ran "The Right Wing Is Rallying Around Novak Djokovic Over Vaccine Stance," while "Axios" referred to the controversy simply as "The Djokovic Debacle."

The consequences for Djokovic extended beyond media criticism. Because Australia canceled his visa before the 2022 Australian Open, he was deported and unable to compete. United States travel requirements also prevented him from entering the country for several major tournaments, including Indian Wells, the Miami Open, and the 2022 U.S. Open.

The mistreatment of Djokovic cost him millions of dollars and potentially a major or two. It objectively affected the record books and his pocketbook.

The apology from tennis and mainstream media should be just as loud as the criticism, but I’m not expecting it.

The then Detroit Red Wings forward Tyler Bertuzzi became one of the NHL's most recognizable unvaxxed players. For a time, Bertuzzi was only one of four unvaxxed players in the league, but eventually become the only unvaxxed player when others folded.

Unlike some athletes who frequently discussed vaccine policy, Bertuzzi offered little public commentary beyond confirming that he had chosen not to be vaccinated. Bertuzzi said, "It’s a personal choice, freedom of choice, and life choice."

What made his case so special is the fact that he’s Canadian. Because of his lack of vaccination, he wasn’t allowed to play in or travel to his home country during the season.

The NHL never required players to receive the COVID-19 vaccine. However, Canada's border policy at the time prohibited most unvaxxed foreign nationals from entering the country. As a result, Bertuzzi missed every regular-season game played in Canada during the 2021-22 season and forfeited the salary associated with those games. Missing those games up north reportedly cost him around half a million dollars. It was another courageous stance financially and ethically.

The media labeled his decision as "short-sighted and selfish." We have yet to hear one hockey media member or outlet apologize to Bertuzzi for the way he was vilified during that season.

SWITZERLAND FIRES HOCKEY COACH WHO ADMITTED TO FAKING VACCINATION STATUS FOR 2022 BEIJING OLYMPICS

The now retired, former Buffalo Bills wide receiver Cole Beasley emerged as perhaps the NFL's most outspoken critic of COVID-19 vaccine mandates, along with Aaron Rodgers.

Unlike many players who kept their decisions private, Beasley openly challenged league policies and defended players' right to make their own medical decisions. Among his most widely quoted comments were, "I'll be out in public. If you're scared of me, then steer clear," and "I'll live my one life like I want to."

Those statements generated enormous media attention. ESPN, CNN, and countless newspapers and opinion writers regularly covered Beasley's comments. Outlets criticized him for questioning vaccine policies or argued that he was sending the wrong message to fans.

While the NFL did not require players to be vaccinated, they made life very difficult for those who refused. The league established different protocols based on vaccination status. Unvaxxed players were subject to daily COVID testing, masking requirements, travel restrictions, quarantine following exposure, and additional limitations inside team facilities.

Beasley called out the league for holding him out of crucial game against the New England Patriots in December 2021 because he tested positive for COVID, calling out the double standard of how "vaxxed players are playing with COVID every week now because they (NFL) don’t test."

The NFL also warned that teams experiencing outbreaks among unvaxxed players could potentially forfeit games if contests could not be rescheduled. Beasley frequently argued that these policies effectively pressured players into receiving the vaccine despite there being no formal mandate.

No media member or outlet has publicly apologized to him. Not shocked.

ANTHONY FAUCI’S LAWYER SAYS AARON RODGERS 'SHOULD STICK TO FOOTBALL’ AFTER SCORCHING HIM ON PAT MCAFEE'S SHOW

Orlando Magic forward Jonathan Isaac became one of the NBA's most prominent voices defending individual choice during the pandemic, after becoming a cultural lightning rod for refusing to kneel for the anthem in the NBA Bubble.

At the NBA's 2021 Media Day, Isaac stated, "I am not anti-vax. I'm not anti-medicine." He also explained, "I don't think being unvaccinated means infected or infectious," and said that after recovering from COVID-19 himself, he believed natural immunity played a role in his personal decision. Wow. What a concept.

His press conference quickly became one of the most widely discussed media sessions of the NBA season.

Many of his critics in the media claimed he was anti-science, selfish, and spewing right-wing propaganda.

"Rolling Stone," which claimed Kyrie Irving was a conspiracy theorist, also named Isaac for his anti-vax stance. Isaac’s comments were quoted in the "Rolling Stone" report, which concluded Isaac refused the vaccine after watching Trump press conferences. Isaac destroyed that claim the first chance he got, stating that he was "badly misrepresented."

Unlike some professional leagues, the NBA never implemented a league-wide vaccine mandate. Instead, local government rules created different circumstances for players depending on where they played. New York City's vaccine requirement prevented unvaccinated home players from participating in games, which most notably affected Brooklyn Nets guard Kyrie Irving.

Isaac, however, played in Florida, where no comparable local mandate prevented him from competing. While he remained subject to the NBA's COVID protocols for unvaccinated players, he was never suspended or barred from playing solely because of his vaccination status.

While he didn’t suffer financially like Irving, Isaac was a bold voice who received a lot of vitriol from the media. Still, no apologies have been offered, though I believe they are deserved.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Each athlete became the subject of intense public debate, and each received significant criticism from portions of the media. Some lost massive amounts of money for their bold stances. All four athletes consistently framed their decisions as matters of personal choice rather than opposition to medicine itself. Their experiences became defining examples of how sports, politics, public health, and individual liberty intersected during one of the most polarizing periods in modern sports history.

These athletes deserve our love and respect. They were catalysts for change and encouraged countless Americans and Canadians to stand firm in their convictions.

While I don’t expect to see media members and outlets take Stephen A. Smith’s lead in taking accountability and humbling themselves in regards to the covid vaccine, we can at least find solace in the fact one courageous athlete has received his flowers.

item.title: Maryland's lone congressional Republican blasts Moore's redistricting push as alleged 2028 White House play
item.description: Rep. Andy Harris claims Gov. Wes Moore is pushing a Maryland ballot amendment to eliminate his district in furtherance of presidential ambitions.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., the only Republican in Maryland's congressional delegation, is accusing Gov. Wes Moore of backing an amendment to the state constitution that could eliminate his district through redistricting, arguing that the push is driven by the governor's alleged presidential ambitions.

The amendment, if approved by voters in November, would give the Democratic-controlled General Assembly far greater latitude to redraw the state's congressional districts ahead of the 2028 election.

"The governor certainly led the charge in trying to eliminate the only Republican in the Maryland delegation in furtherance of his presidential aspirations," Harris told Fox News Digital in an interview. "It's obvious that this is not being done for Maryland, it is being done for a national agenda."

Moore has repeatedly said he is not running for president in 2028. but speculation around his potential White House bid remains.

TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT OUSTED IN HOUSE PRIMARY AS GOP REDISTRICTING PUSH SET TO RESHAPE TENNESSEE

Harris also called out Moore for engaging in a "photo-op" on Wednesday by publicly signing the bill that will put the amendment on the ballot this fall.

The bill passed Tuesday with three-fifths majorities in both chambers, which is the only requirement for an amendment to become a ballot question, according to Article XIV of the Maryland Constitution.

"Gov. Moore, never missing a photo op for his presidential aspirations, convened a signing ceremony, which is a little unusual considering there's really nothing to sign for the governor," Harris said. "But again, this is all for show. This is to make sure that he can look Gavin Newsom in the eye and say, 'Yeah I did something too for mid-cycle redistricting.'"

Fox News Digital reached out to Moore's office for comment.

Harris, who worked as an anesthesiologist before getting into politics, has represented Maryland's first congressional district since 2011. The district contains the entire Eastern Shore, a relatively rural part of the state, as well as parts of Baltimore County.

VIRGINIA VOTERS CEMENT SWING DISTRICT REMATCH AFTER DEMS’ REDISTRICTING FAIL

The proposed amendment Harris is fighting against could allow state lawmakers to carve up his district and make it untenable for a Republican to win.

As it stands, the Maryland Constitution requires General Assembly districts and U.S. House districts to respect natural boundaries and existing county and municipal lines.

The amendment would remove those requirements for congressional districts while leaving them in place for state legislative districts.

"It absolutely sets up a double standard for redistricting in the state of Maryland. And again, the blatant attempt is to eliminate the Republican representation," Harris said.

MARYLAND BALLOT BLUNDER SPARKS HOUSE GOP PROBE AHEAD OF PRIMARY

The amendment is already facing a court challenge from the Oversight Project, a conservative watchdog group that filed a complaint Thursday night in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court seeking to keep it off the November ballot.

The Oversight Project accused state legislators of bypassing the established July 1 deadline to introduce statewide ballot questions.

The ballot question for the amendment was introduced by Maryland House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk and Senate President Bill Ferguson on Aug. 3, more than a month after the deadline.

Fox News Digital reached out to Peña-Melnyk and Ferguson for comment.

The move by Peña-Melnyk and Ferguson at the tail end of the legislative session is a response to a 2022 court ruling that struck down Democratic lawmakers’ proposed congressional map at the time.

Judge Lynne Battaglia found that the map — which added more Democratic voters to Harris' district — failed to give sufficient regard to the natural boundaries and political subdivisions throughout the state.

TWIN COURT RULINGS RESHAPE HOUSE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS FIGHT UPHILL REDISTRICTING BATTLE

Amending the state constitution could be a way to get around this, but Harris said that even if voters approve the amendment, it would not guarantee that the courts would approve subsequently drawn maps that have "hyper-partisan gerrymandering."

If the state legislature tried to eliminate or substantially dilute Republican voting power his district, Harris said he would sue based on the precedent set by Battaglia's 2022 ruling.

Meanwhile, Moore has framed his support of the amendment as a necessary response to GOP redistricting around the country, which he called "political redlining."

"For over a year, I have warned that Donald Trump and Republicans across the country are working to rig the system, weaken voting rights, and make this pain permanent. I am proud that today we united and took action," Moore said. "I continue to believe that our country needs national redistricting reform. But until that happens, inaction is not an option."

DEMOCRATS TARGETING 12 ADDITIONAL RED DISTRICTS IN MIDTERMS PUSH TO RETAKE HOUSE

Harris pushed back on Moore's assertion that Republicans are responsible for the current redistricting battle playing out in dozens of states.

He pointed out that the redistricting organization founded by Eric Holder, who served as attorney general under President Obama from 2009 to 2015, aggressively pursued litigation to change legislative and congressional maps in North Carolina and Alabama.

However, a mid-decade congressional redraw was successfully enacted by Texas Republicans in 2003. The Supreme Court largely upheld the redraw in 2006 but said one district violated the Voting Rights Act because it diluted Latino voting strength.

Although courts have upheld the legality of redrawing congressional maps between the decennial censuses, Harris said he would like to move away from the practice in the future.

"I don't think it is good for anyone," Harris said. "It's not good for democracy. You get to know your constituents, your constituents get to know their representative. That's important in a representative government like we have."

item.title: Detroit-area couple accused of throwing explosive device with alarming 2-word message into neighbor's yard
item.description: Jason and Megan Showers face decades in prison after allegedly throwing an explosive device marked "BYE BYE" into their 72-year-old neighbor's yard.
item.content:encoded:
A couple living in the suburbs of Detroit has been accused of throwing an explosive device with a chilling two-word message into their neighbor's yard, local prosecutors said.

Jason Showers, 45, and his wife, Megan Showers, 38, both of St. Clair Shores, Michigan, each face decades in prison if they are convicted of charges tied to the Monday incident, according to the Macomb County Prosecutor's Office.

Prosecutors said Megan Showers lit the explosive — described as a red, cylindrical device with the words "BYE BYE" on it — before Jason Showers tossed it into their 72-year-old neighbor's yard.

The neighbor was able to extinguish the explosive, authorities said.

MISSOURI NEIGHBOR ACCUSED OF KILLING MOTHER AND TEEN DAUGHTER AFTER CONFRONTING FAMILY OVER DISPUTE

Law enforcement officials later searched the Showers' home, finding "firearms, ammunition, and materials for assembling explosive devices," according to prosecutors.

"The allegations in this case are serious and especially troubling because they involve a senior member of our community. My office is committed to protecting public safety and prosecuting cases where individuals are accused of endangering others," Macomb County prosecutor Peter Lucido said in a statement.

Jason and Megan Showers are charged with placing explosives near property and possessing bombs with unlawful intent, both felonies that each carry a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.

DOJ ARRESTS MAN ACCUSED OF PROVIDING GUN USED BY FATHER WHO ALLEGEDLY KILLED EIGHT CHILDREN

Jason Showers also faces charges of being a prohibited person in possession of a firearm and ammunition, each punishable by up to five years in prison.

On top of that, prosecutors charged him with two counts of felony firearm possession, with each count carrying a mandatory two-year sentence that must be served consecutively to the underlying felony if he is convicted.

Since Jason Showers is a habitual offender with at least four prior felony convictions, the judge will be able to impose a life sentence if he is convicted of any one of the four top charges, prosecutors said.

OLD TRAILS FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED TO SETTING 25 FIRES; JUDGE DOUBLES BAIL TO $2M

The couple made their first appearance in court on Wednesday, public records show. Their first probable cause hearing is scheduled for Aug. 14.

The judge granted Jason Showers a $100,000 cash-only bond. However, records show that he is still behind bars at the Macomb County Jail.

If he posts bond, he would have to wear a steel cuff GPS tether, the judge ordered. He would also be prohibited from returning to his home or having any contact with his wife or the neighbor.

Megan Showers' bond was set at $20,000, but the judge gave her the ability to pay 10% through a bail bondsman, prosecutors said.

The judge said she could return to her marital home, but she cannot have contact with her husband or the neighbor.

item.title: Congress must fix the Protect College Sports Act before girls pay the price
item.description: Alliance Defending Freedom warns the Protect College Sports Act could undermine 27 state laws keeping men out of women's sports despite its intent.
item.content:encoded:
When legislators started hearing that men were competing in girls’ sports, they acted. Twenty-seven states passed laws that said, in effect: Not on my watch. Our girls have equal opportunity, and they will not be sidelined in their own sports. But a federal bill now moving through Congress could undo what those legislators, and the girls who stood up alongside them, fought to win.

At Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF), we have been in the thick of that fight for the better part of a decade. We stood beside our client, Selina Soule, and her Connecticut teammates as they were forced to race against males and watched 15 girls’ state titles handed to male competitors. Theirs was the first lawsuit of many.

We celebrated as President Donald Trump signed a groundbreaking executive order recognizing the biological truth of male and female and directing the federal government to keep men out of women’s sports.

THE "PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT" HAS A FATAL FLAW: IT DOESN’T PROTECT WOMEN | RILEY GAINES

And most recently, alongside Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey, we represented three female athletes in Idaho and West Virginia whose cases reached the Supreme Court. On June 30, we won. The Supreme Court upheld both states’ laws and confirmed what most Americans already know: an athlete’s sex matters, and states can keep girls’ sports for girls.

But that win came only after years of devastating losses. In West Virginia alone, one boy displaced over 470 girls more than 1,400 times, including by taking a state championship. We know this terrain because we have walked it, legislature by legislature, courtroom by courtroom, for years.

So when I raise concerns about the Protect College Sports Act’s potential effect on state laws protecting women’s sports, I do so as someone who has helped litigate these cases, not as someone watching from the stands.

I do not doubt that Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and his co-sponsors want to protect the integrity of college sports. But good intentions don’t win lawsuits. Precise language does. And the language in this bill, as written, is loose enough for an enterprising judge to make all sorts of mischief. It also gives far too much power to the NCAA, which has betrayed women and girls for years.

TRUMP URGES CONGRESS TO PASS PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE RECESS: 'WE HAVE TO GET THAT DONE'

The Protect College Sports Act, a bill about NIL deals and player transfers, sets general nationwide collegiate eligibility rules and then limits the ability of states to address eligibility. Yet many of the state sports laws say that sex-based classifications implicate eligibility and declare men ineligible for women’s teams. A hostile administration or an activist judge could twist the bill’s language to argue that every state law that keeps men out of women’s sports is unenforceable. The bill also doesn’t fully safeguard Title IX—which authorizes separate teams, locker rooms and showers for girls.

At ADF, we’ve been warning Congress about the unnecessary risk posed by this bill for weeks. We’ve even offered a simple fix that would minimize the risk of undoing women’s sports laws. And time and again, our solution has been ignored.

It almost seems as if this is just another instance of society prioritizing men over women. The bill’s main purpose is to fix the money and chaos in the men’s games, especially football, where the dollars are. That is what its sponsors care to fix. Whether the fix endangers girls is not the highest priority. Once again, when men’s and women’s interests share a page, the women’s side absorbs the risk.

None of that is what the bill’s drafters intend. But intent is not what a court enforces, and I have spent a legal career watching lawyers seize on every ambiguous phrase they can find. Twenty years ago, no one thought we would need to define what a woman is.

REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS

There is no room for ambiguity. When the stakes are our daughters’ rights on the field and in the locker room, "probably fine" is not good enough. Having fought these battles, I know how the sequel ends: back in court for another decade, defending ground we already won, while female athletes pay the price.

The rights of girls should not depend on how some future court chooses to read a sentence Congress left unclear. Nearly eight in 10 Americans agree that men do not belong in women’s sports. That is not a fringe position, and it is no longer a partisan one. Truth does not have a party affiliation, and fairness for female athletes never should.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The fix is simple: tighten the language to unambiguously ensure that state women’s sports laws are not preempted and that Title IX remains untouched. Sponsors can address athlete compensation while ensuring states can keep men out of women’s sports. Those goals are not in tension. Until Congress passes a bill that protects women’s sports in all 50 states, it should make sure that no legislation undermines the 27 states with the courage to act—and that the defenders of women’s sports remain free to make the case that the other 23 should follow.

We just won a landmark ruling for women and girls. Let’s not shoot ourselves in the foot by handing the other side a tool we know they will misuse. Let’s not enact permanent legislation that unravels the Trump administration’s work to defend biological truth in sports or ignites another round of costly litigation pushing for men to compete in women’s sports.

A bill that claims to protect sports should protect the girls who play them. Clean up the language by making it clear the law doesn’t preempt state laws that keep men out of women’s sports. Don’t force us to bear the risk of losing the ground we’ve gained.

item.title: Conor McGregor has surgery on torn ACL, again vows comeback: 'My knee is repaired...Thank you God'
item.description: Conor McGregor posted a video confirming his ACL surgery was a success, naming Dominick Cruz, Georges St. Pierre, and Tom Brady as motivation.
item.content:encoded:
Conor McGregor is on the road to recovery after his return to the Octagon barely lasted one minute.

After five years without a fight, McGregor opened his July 11 fight against Max Holloway aggressively, attempting a running kick before throwing a head kick moments later. However, he slipped both times because it was apparent he had suffered a knee injury.

He tried to power through it, but nearly two minutes into the fight, he grabbed at his right leg again, and referee Mike Beltran called the fight after just 69 seconds following what ultimately was a torn ACL.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

McGregor, though, posted a video to social media saying that his surgery was a "success."

"What’s up, folks? The Mac is back, baby. My knee is repaired, surgery was a success, and I’m on the road to recovery. That should tell you all you need to know about my mindset. Straight into surgery, knee repaired, and on the road. Let’s go," he said in the video.

McGregor then name-dropped former fighters Dominick Cruz and Georges St. Pierre, as well as Tom Brady and Adrian Peterson, other athletes who have returned from ACL tears, as his "motivation...especially the fighting boys."

"My mindset is unstoppable, unbreakable. Thank you God. Thank you so much God."

McGregor vowed shortly after the injury that he would be back.

WHY CONOR MCGREGOR CALLS HIS EXACT KNEE INJURY 'QUITE SHOCKING' AFTER FINDING OUT RESULTS

"We'll be back... In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen. We'll be back. Let's go."

McGregor made an emotional post the day after the fight, saying his "head gasket is gone."

"Destroyed. I had no injury / injuries going into the fight. I was throwing kicks, planted and jumping, all throughout camp as well as backstage before the fight. This came out of nowhere. I am beyond dark here. I can only describe it as hell," he said on X.

McGregor was participating in his first bout since July 2021 when he lost to Dustin Poirier due to a devastating leg injury. He’s only won one fight since 2020.
